en: Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga Pācittiyakaṇḍa
Sappāṇakavagga 70.
The Training Rule on Thorns.
At that time the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, a certain novice named Kaṇṭaka had developed such an evil view as this:
"As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called 'obstructive states' by the Blessed One are not actually capable of being obstacles for one who indulges in them.
A number of bhikkhus heard it said that such an evil view had arisen in the novice named Kaṇṭaka.
“I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that these things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
Then those bhikkhus went to the novice Kaṇṭaka and, having approached him, said this to the novice Kaṇṭaka:
“Is it true, friend Kaṇṭaka, that such an evil view as this has arisen in you?”
“Do you understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that those things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them?

“I do indeed, Bhante, understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in this way: ‘Those things called obstructive states by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
“Do not say so, friend Kaṇṭaka! Do not misrepresent the Blessed One. It is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One; the Blessed One would never speak in such a manner.”
"In many ways, friend Kaṇṭaka, the Blessed One has stated that obstructive things are indeed obstacles. They are sufficient to become an obstacle for one who indulges in them.
The Blessed One has stated that sensual pleasures provide little gratification, but much suffering and much despair; the danger here is greater still...
[and so on]. Even though the novice Kaṇṭaka was being addressed by those monks in this way, he stubbornly and dogmatically clung to that evil view and continued to assert it.

“Venerable sir, it is in this way that I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One: ‘Those things called obstructions by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
But when those bhikkhus were unable to detach the novice Kaṇṭaka from that evil speculative view, they approached the Blessed One. Having approached, they [reported this to] the Blessed One...
They reported this matter to him.
Then, on that occasion and for that reason, the Blessed One had the community of monks assembled and questioned the novice Kaṇṭaka:
“Is it true, Kaṇṭaka, that such an evil course of view has arisen in you?”

“Do you really understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in such a way that those things called ‘obstructive states’ by the Blessed One are not actually able to obstruct one who indulges in them?
“I do indeed understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One in this way, venerable sir: ‘Those things called obstructive states by the Blessed One are not able to obstruct one who indulges in them.
“Whom, you foolish man, do you think I have taught the Dhamma in such a way?”
"Is it not true, you foolish man, that I have in many ways declared sensual pleasures to be obstructive conditions, sufficient to become an obstacle for one who indulges in them?
I have declared sensual pleasures to be of little gratification, full of suffering, and full of despair; the danger therein is greater still.
I have declared sensual pleasures to be like a skeleton... [and so on].
"Sensual pleasures have been compared by me to the head of a snake; they bring much suffering and much despair, and the danger therein is even greater.
Yet you, foolish man, by your own misapprehension, misrepresent both us and destroy yourself, and you generate much demerit.
For that, foolish man, will lead to your harm and suffering for a long time."
“O foolish man, this does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
nor to the increase of confidence in some of those who already have it.
Having rebuked him... [the Buddha continued].
Having given a discourse on the Dhamma, he addressed the bhikkhus:
“In that case, bhikkhus, let the Saṅgha expel the novice Kaṇṭaka.
And thus, bhikkhus, should he be expelled:”
“From this day forward, friend Kaṇṭaka, you shall no longer refer to that Blessed One as your teacher.
Furthermore, you shall no longer have the privilege of sharing a sleeping place with the bhikkhus for two or three nights, which other novice monks receive.
Go away! Depart! Be gone!”
Then the Saṅgha expelled the novice Kaṇṭaka.
At that time, the group-of-six monks, knowing that the novice Kaṇṭaka had been thus expelled, befriended him, attended upon him, ate with him, and even shared a sleeping place with him.
Those monks who were of few desires... [as before]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“How can the group-of-six monks, knowing that the novice Kaṇṭaka has been thus expelled, still support him, attend upon him, eat together with him, and even share a sleeping place with him?
… [The Buddha said: “Is it true, monks, that you, knowing that the novice Kaṇṭaka has been thus expelled, support him, attend upon him, eat together with him, and share a sleeping place with him?
“It is true, Blessed One.”
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them:

“… How can you, foolish men, knowing that the novice Kaṇṭaka has been expelled by the Saṅgha, still provide him with food, attend to him, eat together with him, and even share a sleeping place with him?
This, foolish men, will not lead to the confidence of those without confidence…” [and so on].
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:
“If a novice should speak thus:

‘As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things called “obstructive states” by the Blessed One are not sufficient to be an obstruction for one who indulges in them,’ [he should be dealt with accordingly].”
That novice monk should be addressed by the monks thus:
“Friend novice, do not speak thus; do not misrepresent the Blessed One, for it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One, and the Blessed One would not say such a thing.
Friend novice, in many ways the obstructive states have been declared by the Blessed One to be obstructive. It is sufficient that they should become an obstruction for one who indulges in them.”
And if that novice, being thus addressed by the monks, should still persist as before, that novice is to be told by the monks:
“Friend novice, from this day forward, you may no longer point to the Blessed One as your teacher.
Furthermore, you no longer have the privilege of sharing a sleeping place with the monks for two or three nights, which other novices enjoy.”
"Go away, you wretch!

Be gone! Yet, if a monk, knowing that a novice has been thus expelled, should support him, or attend upon him, or eat together with him, or share a sleeping place with him, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
As for "novice": [the definition follows].
He is called a novice (sāmaṇera).
He should speak thus:

"As I understand the Dhamma taught by the Blessed One, those things which have been declared by the Blessed One to be obstructive conditions are not sufficient to constitute an obstruction for one who indulges in them."
"Thus, 'the novice' refers to that novice who speaks in such a manner.
'By the monks'..."
Other monks who see or hear this should say to him: "Friend novice, do not speak thus. Do not misrepresent the Blessed One;
it is not good to misrepresent the Blessed One. The Blessed One would not speak in such a way.
Friend novice, in many ways the Blessed One has stated that obstructive things are indeed obstructive. It is sufficient for them to be an obstruction for one who indulges in them."
A second time he should be addressed...
a third time he should be addressed.
If he relinquishes it, that is well; if he does not relinquish it, that novice monk should be addressed by the monks as follows:
“From this day forward, friend novice, you shall no longer point to that Blessed One as your teacher.
Furthermore, you shall no longer have the privilege shared by other novices of staying together with the bhikkhus for two or three nights.
Go away! Depart! Be gone!”
"But whoever" means whoever such [a person]...
"monks" means... [as before].
... [as before] ... this is the "bhikkhu" intended in this context.
"Knows" means he knows by himself, or others inform him, or he informs [others].
"Thus expelled" means expelled in this manner.
"A novice" (samaṇuddesa) is so named...
A novice is what is meant.
"Should entice" means:
if he entices him with the thought, "I will give him his bowl or his robe, or a recitation, or an interrogation," there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"Or should attend upon him" means:
if he consents to [receiving] powder, clay, tooth-sticks, or mouth-water from him, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
"Or should associate with him" means:
What is called "enjoyment" consists of two kinds of enjoyment:
the enjoyment of material goods and the enjoyment of the Dhamma.
The enjoyment of material goods is as follows:
If she gives or receives material goods, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
What is called "partaking of the Dhamma" means that she recites or causes it to be recited; if she recites or causes it to be recited by the line, there is an offense of expiation for every line.
If he teaches it syllable by syllable or causes it to be taught syllable by syllable, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya) for every syllable.
Or if they share a bed:
when the novice who has been expelled is lying down in a place covered by a single roof, and the monk lies down [with him], there is an offense of expiation.
If a novice monk who has been expelled lies down while a bhikkhu is already lying down, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If both lie down together, there is an offense of expiation.
If they rise up and lie down again and again, there is an offense of expiation for each instance.

If one encourages, supports, shares food with, or lies down in the same bed as one who has been expelled, while perceiving that person to have been expelled, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
If one encourages, supports, shares food with, or lies down in the same bed as one who has been expelled, while being uncertain of their expulsion, there is an offense of wrongdoing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one encourages, supports, shares food with, or lies down in the same bed as one who has been expelled, while perceiving them not to have been expelled, there is no offense.
If it is one who has not been expelled, but he perceives her as expelled, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If it is one who has not been expelled, but he is uncertain about it, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If it is one who has not been expelled, and he perceives her as not expelled, there is no offense.
There is no offense if he knows that [the monk] has not been expelled;
or if he knows that [the monk] has relinquished that view.
"In the case of one who is insane,
and in the case of the first offender.
The tenth training rule concerning thorns is finished.
The seventh chapter: On Living Beings.
Its summary verse:
Intentional killing and [the offense regarding] living beings.
Reopening [a settled case], concealing a grave offense,
[teaching] the Dhamma to one under twenty years of age,
making arrangements [for a journey], and [the offense of] Ariṭṭha.
The thorn that has been pulled out,
and these ten training rules.
